extracted.intended_audience: PR practitioners, marketers, communications professionals, and anyone who writes press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on optimal press release word count, page length, and structural/formatting practices to maximize readability and media pickup. Covers when shorter or longer releases are appropriate and common length-related mistakes to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal word count (300–500 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: We generally aim for an ideal word count of 300 to 500 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This range balances clarity and completeness: allows a headline/subheadline, summary, strong lead paragraph, supporting details, one or two attributable quotes, and a boilerplate with contact information. A concise release in this range is more likely to be read fully and picked up by media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-page preferred; two-page maximum
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-page press release is ideal for most announcements. When the news is complex, a two-page maximum is acceptable but should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer releases risk losing media interest and reader attention. Keep to one page where possible; only expand to two pages for legitimately complex stories that cannot be summarized succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short releases for quick announcements (<300 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief press releases under 300 words suit quick announcements, event reminders, or simple updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are easy to read and digital-friendly but must still include all essential information (clear headline, lead with key facts, and contact info) so journalists have what they need to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long releases for detailed stories (600–1000 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases exceeding ~600 words are considered long and may be necessary for detailed product launches, mergers, or complex stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long releases require careful editing and structure to maintain clarity and media-friendliness. Use them only when necessary and consider supplemental materials (backgrounders, fact sheets) instead of lengthening the main release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the inverted pyramid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the most important information—the who, what, when, where, why, and how—at the beginning. Supporting details and background follow in descending order of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures readers grasp the key message immediately and aligns with journalistic practices, improving chances of media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on essential information; avoid filler and jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to relevant facts, actionable content, and direct language tailored to the target audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruthlessly remove fluff, marketing-speak, and unnecessary detail. Maintaining focus improves clarity and impact; irrelevant tangents dilute the message and waste space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain short paragraphs and sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be 3–4 sentences max, and sentences should be clear and straightforward to enhance readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter paragraphs and sentences increase skimmability and help journalists find facts quickly. Avoid dense blocks of text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ formatting techniques for skimmability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bullet points, numbered lists, subheadings, and white space to break up text and make key points skimmable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good formatting guides the reader through the content and makes it easy for media to extract facts quickly (which increases chances of pickup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit and proofread thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove redundancy, repetition, and wordiness. Ensure the release is polished and professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough editing reduces confusion, eliminates errors that undermine credibility, and helps keep the release within the recommended length. Proofread for grammar, factual accuracy, and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise headline (ideally under 10 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should be concise—ideally under 10 words—capturing the essence of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, short headline quickly conveys the main news point and entices readers. Pairing a strong headline with a brief subheadline (one to two sentences) can add context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a brief summary or deck
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief summary or deck highlights the key message and entices readers to continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place this near the top to provide context and make the lead more compelling; keep it short and focused on the newsworthy angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong lead paragraph with essential facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead paragraph delivers the essential information and sets the tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead answers the who/what/when/where/why/how and hooks the reader; it should be clear, direct, and news-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting details and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context, data, and additional facts to support the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supporting paragraphs to expand on the main points in descending importance. If more in-depth information is needed, provide attachments or links rather than bloating the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include one or two attributable quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include one or two attributable quotes that add perspective or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should be relevant, concise, media-friendly, and directly related to the news without sounding promotional. They add human voice or expert interpretation but should not substitute for factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish with a boilerplate and contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boilerplate offers a brief company overview; contact details enable media follow-up. These elements are essential for journalists to verify and pursue the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose length appropriate to news complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Match release length and depth to the complexity of the announcement (short for simple updates; longer for complex launches or M&A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story is complex, consider supplementary assets (backgrounders, FAQs) instead of extending the main release. Avoid unnecessary length by separating core news from additional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common formatting and focus mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Common pitfalls include excessive length, overly brief releases that omit key facts, lack of focus (irrelevant details), and poor formatting (dense text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these anti-patterns: long releases that bury the message, too-brief releases that leave out essential information, scattered narratives that dilute newsworthiness, and dense formatting that reduces skimmability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make releases media-friendly and scannable
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be concise, media-friendly, and structured for easy scanning to increase the chance of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting, headline quality, inverted pyramid structure, and clarity all contribute to media-friendliness. Respect journalists' time by making key facts immediately accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use even shorter releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases can be shorter than 300 words for quick updates, event reminders, or simple announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even very short releases must still include a clear headline, a lead with key facts, and contact information to remain effective and actionable.
